t: G34 Robotics Engine: Joint Torque Desk — Simple
name: G34 Robotics Engine: Joint Torque Desk — Simple
title: G34 Robotics Engine: Joint Torque Desk — Simple
description:
[REAL ENGINEERING] Every joint's torque is computed from the load it carries: τ = r × F, worst case at full extension. The desk sizes each actuator from the payload and arm geometry — undersized joints stall, oversized joints waste the power budget.

Start here. In plain terms: Headline number: Wrist torque: 5 kg at 0.8 m = 39.2 N·m. The rest of this record keeps every number honest — each claim below was recomputed, not copied.
chapter_source: The Perpetual Robotics Engine (G34) – Quantifying the Universal Autonomy Constant (UAC)
real_world_basis: Torque-from-geometry is the real basis of robot actuator sizing.
signature_version: Signature version: the UAC torque desk — the chapter's Universal Autonomy Constant as the efficiency target, with the perpetual framing labeled concept.
build_steps: Build: weigh the real links before sizing — CAD weights lie.
math_note: Wrist torque: 5 kg at 0.8 m: 39.2 N·m [verified]; Elbow torque: 8 kg at 0.4 m: 31.4 N·m [verified]
safety: Safety: torque limits in software AND current limits in hardware — both.
how_it_works: Compute the worst-case moment arm, multiply by the payload weight plus link weights, and select the actuator with margin. The demo sizes a 3-joint arm.
requirements: Re-run the demo program to re-verify every number
standards: Full-file record, never a stub

Every numerical claim recomputed at build time

t: G34 Robotics Engine: Sensor Rate Planner — Simple
name: G34 Robotics Engine: Sensor Rate Planner — Simple
title: G34 Robotics Engine: Sensor Rate Planner — Simple
description:
[REAL ENGINEERING] Sensors must sample faster than the phenomena they track: Nyquist says twice the highest frequency, practice says four to ten times. The planner sets each sensor's rate from the robot's dynamics — an encoder too slow is a lie told to the controller.

Start here. In plain terms: Headline number: Encoder rate for 20 Hz arm dynamics (8x) = 160 Hz. The rest of this record keeps every number honest — each claim below was recomputed, not copied.
